SEBI's proposed changes to SME IPO rules: The key points

(Public Comments are invited)

On 14 October 2026, SEBI released a consultation paper proposing changes to the rules for IPOs on the SME platform. The proposals draw on a Working Group report, the Primary Market Advisory Committee's views and SEBI's own internal review. Below is a summary of the main changes.

Eligibility





Size test: Eligibility would be based on post-issue market capitalisation at the offer price, instead of post-issue paid-up capital (currently up to ₹10 crore, optionally up to ₹25 crore). Issuers up to ₹1,000 crore would have to list on the SME platform. Issuers between ₹1,000 and ₹4,000 crore could choose it, but would have to present restated financials under Ind AS.



Profitability: Average operating profit of at least ₹3 crore a year over the last three years, replacing ₹1 crore in at least two of the last three years.



Alternative route: Issuers that do not meet the profit test could still list through book building if at least 75% of the net offer is allotted to QIBs. Retail investors would get no more than 10%, and all subscription money would be refunded if the 75% QIB allotment is not achieved.

Application and trading





Minimum application: Four lots of at least ₹25,000 each, or ₹1 lakh. SEBI had raised this to ₹2 lakh in March 2025 to limit participation by smaller retail investors. The paper states that the reduction would operate within a substantially strengthened framework.



Trading lot: One share instead of fixed lots. SEBI notes that about 5% of SME shareholders (by PAN) hold odd lots that cannot be fully sold through the regular market.



Anchor investors: Expressly recognised, up to 60% of the QIB portion in book-built issues.

Issue costs and obligations





Underwriting: The 100% underwriting requirement would be replaced by underwriting of the unsubscribed portion, along with a 90% minimum subscription rule. Underwriting fees averaged about 49.5% of total issue expenses for NSE SME IPOs in FY25.



Market making: The compulsory three-year market-making requirement would be removed. Between August 2025 and July 2026, market makers accounted for 0–10% of total turnover in 361 NSE and 268 BSE SME stocks.



General corporate purposes: The ₹10 crore cap would be removed; the 15% limit would stay.

Promoters and existing shareholders





Pre-IPO shareholders (other than the promoter group): Lock-in reduced from one year to six months after allotment. The promoter group would have a one-year lock-in.



Promoters: Holdings above the minimum contribution would be locked in for one year, instead of half for two years and half for one.



Offer for sale: Sellers would need to have held their shares for one year before the draft offer document is filed. QIB sellers would be exempt from the 20%-of-issue and 50%-of-holding caps, except under the alternative route.

Points for investors to note

If adopted, three details in an offer document become relevant. First, the eligibility route: An issue under the 75%-QIB route means the issuer did not meet the ₹3 crore profit test. Second, lock-in dates: Most pre-IPO shareholders could sell six months after allotment. Third, liquidity: Without a designated market maker, trading would depend on regular market participants.

Status

These are proposals, not final rules. Once the final rules are notified, issuers filing draft offer documents in the following three months could choose either framework; after that, the new rules would apply.

Public comments

SEBI is accepting comments until 4 November 2026 through its portal: https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebiweb/publiccommentv2/PublicCommentAction.do?doPublicComments=yes. 

Select the paper ending "related to IPO by SMEs". The form goes through each proposal: Answer Yes or No with reasons, or choose "Skip this proposal". 

Educational, not investment advice.

In each of the last two years, India's listed home-builders sold less in July–September than in April–June. Combined, their Q2 pre-sales were 29% and 28% below Q1.

Their collections went the other way, up 6% and 8%. Buyers pay on construction milestones, not on the calendar. What really moves quarterly sales is when big projects launch.

FY27 looks different so far. Q1 launches were held back, one Gurugram launch has already logged about ₹7,891 crore of allotments, and Nifty Realty is up 2.6% this quarter while the Nifty 50 is down 4.5%.

I've compared eight developers across three years, before any Q2 numbers are out. Part 2 comes after results.

10 minutes or 10 years?

“If you aren’t willing to own a stock for 10 years, don’t even think about owning it for 10 minutes.”

— Warren Buffett

But here’s the uncomfortable question:

Do we really buy businesses, or do we buy prices?

If a stock falls 15% tomorrow, would you still want to own the business?

If the answer is no, perhaps the problem was never the 15% fall.

Maybe we never understood what we were buying.

Long-term investing begins long before the holding period. It begins with understanding the business.

Varmora Granito's grey market premium peaked at ₹15 on 18 September. It is ₹9 today — down 40% before the issue has even opened.

Two new sections go into the Varmora Granito piece today, both because you asked for them. One reports the GMP day-by-day,₹15 at its peak on 18 September, ₹9 now, down 40% before the issue has even opened. The other explains why the market so often ignores the arithmetic.

In August 2021, Exxaro Tiles listed with a grey market premium of ₹4. It closed listing day up 10.3%, almost exactly what the GMP predicted. It trades at ₹6.30 today, 94.8% below its issue price.

The short version: GMP called the direction of listing day right in about 84% of IPOs last year. Of last year's SME listings, only 52.1% are still above their issue price today.

Fed’s bigger message: rates may stay higher for longer

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%, its first hike since 2023, in a unanimous 12–0 decision.

But the rate hike itself was not the biggest signal.

The dot plot shows 16 of 18 Fed officials expect at least one more hike in 2026, pushing the median year-end rate projection to 4.1%.

For Indian markets, this matters because a higher-for-longer US rate environment can keep the US dollar supported, while putting continued pressure on the Indian rupee.

That can translate into:





Higher import costs, particularly for crude oil.



Pressure on companies with significant dollar-denominated costs.



Potential foreign portfolio investment sensitivity to US yields.



Greater attention on the RBI’s room to manage domestic liquidity and rates.

The immediate market takeaway: this was not just a 25-bps hike. It was a signal that the Fed is not yet ready to declare the tightening cycle over.

For Indian investors, the dollar–rupee equation may be just as important as the Fed rate itself.

NSE's share of India's equity options market, measured by premium turnover, has gone 96.86%, 87.43%, 74.71% and now 68.48%. The last of those four is in the RHP filed on 10 September. It was not in the June draft.

Equity options are 60.2% of NSE's revenue from operations. So the largest revenue line is losing share in a market that is itself growing: options revenue still rose 16% in the June quarter, while the slice fell ten percentage points.

Then you reach Note 25. Bill discounting and factoring balances went from ₹42 crore to ₹143 crore in FY26. Strip that increase out and operating cash flow for the year falls from ₹144 crore to about ₹48 crore. After capex, the three years consumed ₹53 crore more cash than they produced.

January to March is the worst quarter for Indian real estate share prices. On the industry's own figures, it is usually one of the busiest quarters for actually selling homes.

I took the five biggest listed property companies and five full years, 2021 to 2025. Nifty Realty averaged −2.4% in January-March and went up in only two of the five years. June went up 76% of the time and July 72%. August was the one month that was reliably weak.

Then I compared it all against the Nifty 50, and most of the pattern vanished. The whole market was down in all five Januarys and up in all five March.

Seven of the twelve monthly patterns disappear if you remove a single year.

Update: the price band is out. ₹1,700 to ₹1,785 a share, lot of 8 shares, bidding 17 to 21 September, listing on BSE on 24 September (per the price-band announcement as reported by Business Standard and IPO trackers). The offer for sale has been trimmed to 12.64 crore shares, about 5.1% of the company, from the 6.02% in the DRHP. NSE still receives nothing.

That fills in the missing variable from Section S. Plugging the upper band into the checklist:

Market cap: ₹1,785 × 247.5 crore shares = about ₹4.42 lakh crore (₹4.21 lakh crore at the lower band).

Trailing P/E: ₹1,785 ÷ ₹41.62 = about 43 times FY2026 earnings (41 times at the lower band). Normalised EPS is roughly the same, so the underlying multiple is similar.

Price to book: about 13.8 times the ₹129.75 book value per share.

Dividend yield on the ₹35 paid for FY2026: about 2%.

The DRHP's disclosed secondary trades earlier this year averaged ₹1,999, so the band sits below where the shares last changed hands privately, and the BSE peer multiple quoted in the DRHP was 66.7 times.

The questions in Section S do not change: what growth in options volumes does 43 times require, how much of that is regulation-dependent, and does the valuation hold under the conservative scenario as well as the optimistic one. Those are for each reader to answer on their own assumptions. Sections O, N and R have the inputs.

Educational, not investment advice.

The world’s biggest derivatives exchange is finally heading towards an IPO.

NSE’s scale is hard to ignore. It accounts for 99.8% of futures trading and 93% of cash-equity trading. Yet there is an interesting detail about this IPO: NSE itself will receive ₹0 from the issue.

That’s because this is a pure Offer for Sale (OFS). Twenty-three existing shareholders are selling shares representing 6.02% of the company.

So the more useful question is: what exactly are investors being offered?

Look beyond the headline market-share numbers and the picture becomes more nuanced. Around 60% of NSE’s revenue comes from equity options, a segment where its market share is relatively weaker and where the regulatory framework continues to evolve.

The RHP also presents some notable numbers: no debt, around ₹34,600 crore in its own treasury investments, and an 84% payout. At the same time, revenue declined 3% in FY2026.

There is, however, one number we don't have yet—and it could change the valuation discussion considerably: the IPO price.

Once the price band is announced, one simple starting point will be:

Trailing P/E = IPO Price ÷ ₹41.62 EPS

For this analysis, I’ve gone through the RHP using my OWNERS framework: Operations, Why the Money, Numbers & Cash, Executives & Promoters, Risks & Rivals, and Sticker Price.

The idea is simple: understand the business first, and only then ask what price the market is being asked to put on it.

This is an educational analysis based on publicly available information and is not investment advice. I am not a SEBI-registered research analyst.

Every IPO week, the same question: "Should I apply?"

Almost nobody asks the one that decides whether you make money over five years: "What am I actually buying, and what am I paying for it?"

A good business, a good IPO and a good price are three different things. A great company can be a poor investment if you overpay. A fairly priced one can be a poor IPO if the proceeds only fund someone's exit.

I wrote a step-by-step guide to keeping the three apart, with a free 21-question test and a calculator. No recommendations, no listing-gain tips. Just how to read the document and decide for yourself.
